title: Early-age mechanical properties and pore structure evolution of concrete incorporating lepidolite slag cured in a combined sodium sulfate–sodium chloride solution
content: Lepidolite slag (LS) is an industrial by-product of lithium ore smelting, with an annual output reaching tens of millions of tons. The effects of a complex salt environment on the pore structure and early-age salt resistance of LS-containing concrete were investigated, with emphasis on the underlying mechanisms. The findings provide a theoretical basis for the large-scale use of LS in construction materials in saline–alkali regions. LS was activated using a mechano-chemical synergistic method. It was then used as a partial replacement for cement at levels of 0%, 10%, 15%, 20%, 25%, and 30%. Specimens were cured for 7 and 28 days under two conditions: simulated complex salt solution (2% Na2SO4 + 1% NaCl) and standard curing. Compressive strength tests and multiple characterization techniques were employed. These included nuclear magnetic resonance (NMR), thermogravimetric-differential thermal analysis (TG-DTG), Fourier transform infrared spectroscopy (FTIR), and scanning electron microscopy (SEM). These methods were used to evaluate the effects of LS content on mechanical properties, pore structure evolution, and hydration products. The mixture containing 20% LS (L20 group) exhibited the best mechanical performance. At 28 days, its compressive strengths under standard and complex salt curing conditions were 27.2 MPa and 20.8 MPa, respectively. These values correspond to increases of 5.4% and 21.6% compared with the control group. Under complex salt curing conditions, the porosity of L20 group was 7.65%, which is 10.7% lower than that of the control group. The proportion of macropores decreased from 80% to 70%. TG-DTG analysis showed that the Ca(OH)2 decomposition peak intensity decreased by approximately 15%. This result indicates that the pozzolanic reaction effectively consumed Ca(OH)2, which is susceptible to chemical attack. FTIR results showed a clear increase in the characteristic peaks of C–S–H gel, suggesting a more compact hydrogen-bonding network. SEM observations confirmed the formation of a dense and homogeneous C–S–H gel structure. Ettringite crystals were smaller and more uniformly distributed. The combined effects of physical filling and pozzolanic reactivity improved the early-age resistance of LS concrete to complex salt attack. Among the replacement levels investigated, 20% LS yielded the highest mean compressive strength. The microstructural results suggest that this performance was associated with the formation of a denser C–S–H gel matrix and the consumption of Ca(OH)2 through pozzolanic reactions. These findings provide experimental evidence for evaluating the early-age performance and selecting mixture proportions of LS concrete intended for use in saline–alkali regions.
